description: Hey, we're 2 college students looking to learn more about interconnections of space and software!
summary: Mars has no roads or GPS, and a single route over steep or loose terrain can strand a rover or end a mission. Kiragam is an interactive 3D Mars route map that helps mission planners and researchers choose safer paths. Built on real NASA and USGS data, it combines an interactive globe with NASA Mars Trek imagery, lets users pick a start and end point in the Gale Crater / Mount Sharp region, and computes a least-cost route that avoids steep slopes using a high-resolution elevation model. It reports distance, maximum and mean slope, and estimated travel time for each route. By making slope-aware planning visual and easy to use, Kiragam supports faster, safer decisions for future missions and shows how open NASA data can become a practical planning tool.
details:
The basis of the program is to find a walkable path between two points selected by the user, optimizing for low steepness. The program uses .tif files that break part of Gale Crater into cells, each containing an elevation value. Using QGIS, the image is cropped to reduce the file size, and the change in elevation across cells is calculated to produce a second .tif file containing the slope of each cell. An A* algorithm finds a pathway from A to B using a cost function that penalizes high steepness. The intended benefit is a program that provides increased safety measures for astronauts exploring Mars, by finding walkable pathways through potentially dangerous terrain. For the backend code relating to data processing and routing, we used Python and the following libraries: rasterio, NumPy, FastAPI, Pydantic, and Uvicorn. For the frontend, we primarily use CesiumJS to display imagery of Mars, and Render hosts our program on a live URL. We wanted to focus on astronaut safety, so the route avoids steep terrain and an average walking speed is used to estimate travel time. We also had to consider memory so that our program didn’t run too long, so we reduced the dimensions of the area for exploration.

In terms of creativity, we stepped outside of our comfort zone by learning new technologies, NASA data, and development tools. We also combined our interests, putting a piece of ourselves into this project. My partner Amrita has recently become very interested in space exploration, especially after the Artemis mission, and this experience allowed her to see where her academic interests in computer science can intersect with her passions. As for me, Avanthika, I have an interest in healthcare technology, so focusing on astronaut safety allowed me to expand on those interests. Overall, our creativity came from bringing our passions for space exploration and healthcare technology together into one tool that reflects who we are and helps keep astronauts safer.
